rv.q: But ultimately one can't argue with the subtlety of the three central performances or the brutal logic of Dyer's production.
As I recall, the last National Theatre ‘Othello’ – from 2013 – didn’t make it about race. Rory Kinnear’s terrifying Iago was happy to viciously slur Adrian Lester’s Moorish general Othello.

We’re left in no doubt about his skills as a warrior — stripped to the waist, he demonstrates his athletic prowess as he wields a staff against a punchball — but this general doesn’t have the ability to turn words into marching columns. He delivers his lines efficiently, like a special adviser, but seldom makes them sing.

In spite of the misfiring conception – one that parts company with any possibility of Othello being a claustrophobic chamber piece – there are outstanding performances to ensure the production torments as it must.
This is a slick, strongly visual yet oddly cold Othello. Fashion trumps sentiment and the verse-speaking is patchy.
That uneasiness, though, is perhaps the triumph of the production.
This version is hot on relevance but it's never ravishing.
His austere staging is bold in its reframing of the play's themes, but sometimes stilted in execution.
Yes, it's a fleet, clear, potent three-hour affair that makes welcome strides for diversity, but it stumbles in some areas.
It's an intense collapse, riding Shakespeare's language to find his own meanings, an extraordinary performance at the heart of a revelatory and relevant production.
His directorial focus is forensic, magnifying the psychodrama at the heart of Shakespeare's play and turning Othello's cognitive turmoil inside out with surgical precision.
Clint Dyer delivers a powerful production with performances both dignified and passionate.
When combined with such rich performances of psychological anguish, this production makes a centuries'-old tale feel vivid and captivating, fresh like a sharp cut.
This is a laudably ambitious production, but one that has jettisoned some of the play's key emotional ballast.

Also, the use of the ensemble – in the programme listed as ‘System’ (whatever that means) – to stay on the stage seated on the steps is a bit distracting at times. As for the four main characters, Terera as Othello is a powerful presence at the centre of the action but then at times, the character comes across as a whiny, manipulating misogynist.
For all the lights, torches and a rumbling sound design that add plenty of atmosphere to Dyer's dystopia, there's a nagging sense that this production is more style than substance.

Some of the visual gestures seem to have been approved by crazies from the neo-fascist fringe. The Moor is first seen doing a work-out with a punch bag but he doesn’t strike the bag, he grabs a broom handle and uses it to perform some fancy martial arts moves.
